passages.happening:
‘Now the Philistines fought against Israel, and the men of Israel fled before them, and many fell slain on Mount Gilboa’ (verse 1). The Philistines kill Saul's sons Jonathan, Abinadab and Malchishua, and archers wound Saul (verses 2-3). Afraid of being taken and tortured, Saul dies by his own hand, and his armor-bearer dies with him (verses 4-5). ‘So Saul died together with his three sons and all his house’ (verse 6). The Israelites in the valley abandon their towns, and the Philistines move in (verse 7).

The next day the Philistines strip the dead, take Saul's armor and his head, and send the news through their land to the temples of their idols (verses 8-10). When the people of Jabesh-gilead hear, their fighting men recover the bodies of Saul and his sons, bury their bones ‘under the oak in Jabesh and fasted seven days’ (verse 12).
passages.hearers:
After nine chapters of names the story begins, and it begins with an ending. The Chronicler tells nothing of Saul's anointing, his early victories or his long conflict with David, which fill 1 Samuel. He tells only Saul's death, and the chapter exists to explain why the kingdom passed to David.

Saul's death is usually placed around 1010 BC. The account follows 1 Samuel 31 closely, with small changes: Samuel says the body was fastened to the wall of Beth-shan, and Chronicles mentions the head in the temple of Dagon, the chief Philistine god. Mount Gilboa rises at the south-east edge of the Jezreel Valley. The Philistines had pushed far north, cutting the hill country off from the northern tribes.

In ancient war a defeated king's body was a trophy; displaying it proclaimed that the victors' gods had won. Burial mattered deeply in Israel, and to be left unburied was a disgrace. The men of Jabesh-gilead had reason to honor Saul: his first act as king had been to rescue their town. They risked their lives to bury him and fasted seven days, the customary time of mourning.
passages.later: In 1 Samuel the same men ‘took their bones and buried them under the tamarisk tree in Jabesh, and they fasted seven days’ (1 Samuel 31:13).
passages.hard:
Saul took his own life. How does the Bible treat this, and what should be said about it?

The text names it in a verse and does not describe it, and these notes do the same. The Bible records a few such deaths, and in each case it reports the act without long comment. It never presents taking one's own life as a good or honorable way out. Here a man in agony, wounded, cut off from God and afraid of torture, is treated with sorrow, not contempt. The men of Jabesh bury him with honor.

Christian traditions have differed on the spiritual state of those who take their own lives. Many have taught that it is a grave sin against God's gift of life, while insisting that salvation rests on Christ's grace and not on the manner of a person's death, and that despair and anguish of mind must be met with compassion. The chapter is not a pattern to follow. It is a tragedy to grieve.

If you have thoughts of hurting yourself, speak to someone today: a doctor, a pastor, a trusted friend, or a crisis line in your country. If you are in danger right now, call your local emergency number. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.
passages.asks: The men of Jabesh remembered what Saul had once done for them, and honored him in death. Ask whose past kindness to you you have forgotten in the light of how their story ended. And ask who near you is in anguish and needs someone to stay with them.

passages.t: Why the kingdom passed to David
passages.happening: ‘So Saul died for his unfaithfulness to the LORD, because he did not keep the word of the LORD and even consulted a medium for guidance’ (verse 13), ‘and he failed to inquire of the LORD. So the LORD put him to death and turned the kingdom over to David son of Jesse’ (verse 14).
passages.hearers:
These two verses are the Chronicler's own verdict, among the most important in the book, because they set out his theology in miniature. Saul was unfaithful, ma'al, the word for Judah's sin that led to exile. He did not keep the word of the LORD. He consulted a medium, which the law forbade and which Saul himself had once driven out of the land. And he did not seek, darash, the LORD.

Darash may be the single most important verb in Chronicles. To seek the LORD is to turn to him in worship, prayer and obedience, to make him one's first resort. Saul was seeking, but in the wrong place. The good kings who follow will be measured by whether they sought him. There is a wordplay too: Saul's name, Shaul, comes from the verb shaal, to ask. The man whose name meant asked for asked the wrong source.
passages.later: The law forbade anyone who ‘consults a medium or spiritist, or inquires of the dead’ (Deuteronomy 18:11).
passages.hard:
The Chronicler says that Saul did not inquire of the LORD, but 1 Samuel 28:6 says that Saul inquired and the LORD did not answer. Do the accounts contradict each other?

First Samuel says that Saul inquired of the LORD, but the LORD did not answer him by dreams, by Urim or by prophets. Chronicles says that he failed to inquire of the LORD. Readers handle this in several ways. Many note that the two books use different verbs: Samuel uses shaal, to ask, while Chronicles uses darash, to seek, which in Chronicles means wholehearted devotion. On this reading Saul asked for information in a crisis but never sought the LORD in the covenant sense of turning to him in obedience and trust, and his quick move to a medium when God was silent shows where his heart lay. Others see the Chronicler giving a verdict on Saul's whole reign rather than on one moment. Either way, the Chronicler is not denying that Saul made an inquiry. He is judging that Saul's life was not one of seeking God.
passages.asks: Saul was seeking, but in the wrong place. Ask where you turn first when God seems silent. And ask whether you are asking God for information, or seeking him.
